newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia holds re-vote on Madura but turnout low.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia holds re-vote on Madura but turnout low.

text.p: Indonesia held an unprecedented re-vote on Madura island on Wednesday but staunch Moslems who had alleged fraud in last week's general elections appeared to have mainly stayed away from the polls.
The re-vote was held in Sampang district on the island off East Java.

It was ordered after supporters of the Moslem-backed United Development Party (PPP) went on a rampage after the May 29 elections and burned ballot boxes on reports that the ruling Golkar party was sweeping the polls.
At the number six booth in Rongtengah, an area of Sampang with a number of Islamic schools, the head of the booth, Fattah, said there were 531 registered voters, of whom 506 voted last week.
On Wednesday, the only voters were the eight officials at the booth itself.
"I don't know why they didn't come. The eight votes were only those of the polling station officials and witnesses," Fattah told Reuters.
Other polling stations had more voters but the overall turnout appeared to be sharply down. The official results were to be released in Surabaya, the main city in East Java, on Thursday.

Golkar, in power for most of President Suharto's 30-year rule, swept last week's national vote with more than 74 percent of the vote. The PPP took just under 23 percent and the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), the only other party entitled to contest the polls, won three percent.

The government imposed tight military and police security on Madura to prevent a recurrence of last week's rioting, in which offices, homes, shops and a church were burned or damaged and polling boxes from Sampang destroyed.
East Java military commander Major-General Imam Utomo had issued a shoot-on-the-spot order in case of further violence, the official Antara news agency reported.

In Jakarta, the PPP and the PDI said they had witnessed a number of irregularities in last week's election, in which nearly 90 percent of the 125 million eligible voters cast their ballots by official count.
The 27-day election campaign also saw the worst political violence in three decades, primarily between supporters of the PPP and Golkar.
Financial markets were carefully monitoring the actions of the PPP, which was due to meet on Thursday to decide whether to accept the election result, for fear of further violence.
Sampang, a sleepy coastal town of about 100,000 people, was quiet on Wednesday under heavy security. The central market and many shops were closed, with shopkeepers saying they feared more trouble.

Officials originally said the re-vote, unprecedented in Indonesia's electoral history, would be held at 86 polling stations. But the head of the Sampang regency, Fadhilah Budiono, said they had found records for 21 of the boxes believed destroyed.
The local secretary of the PPP's Sampang branch, Hasan Asy'ari, who had earlier called for a re-vote throughout the regency, was not at all happy at Budiono's statement.
"I feel like we have been deceived," he said.
The PPP had said it would not supply witnesses for Wednesday's re-vote, though it stopped short of calling for an illegal boycott.
It appeared that polling booth officers were hauling in passers-by to act as witnesses to make up the numbers.

At an intersection about 50 metres (yards) from the Rongtengah booth, a large cardboard sign said: "ABRI (the Indonesian military) wants to take something dishonestly, so please go ahead and have your re-vote with your tight security. The PPP will take a rest. The PPP is not just small talk."
